traveler: Peter of Ravenna (Pietro Francesco Tomai, Petrus Ravennas)
title: A Hundred Thousand Rooms: the Jurist Who Put the Art of Memory on Sale
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Ravenna and the Schools of Padua

stops.name: Ravenna, born to Gioacchino Tomai
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Treccani gives the birth as around 1448 and names the father Gioacchino [A]; no baptismal record, no address, no mother's name survives in modern biography [gap]. The research pool's claim that the father had died by about 1467 appears in no consulted source (Treccani, ADB, NDB, en/it/de Wikipedia) and is not carried here [R, dropped].
stops.campa: In the old Byzantine capital on the drained marsh a son is born to Gioacchino Tomai, and is given the name Pietro Francesco. No baptismal register survives him and no house is pointed out; his mother's name is not preserved in any modern biography, and the year itself is an estimate worked backward from the dates of his degrees. He will be known across Europe by the city and not by the family: Petrus Ravennas, the man from Ravenna, Pietro da Ravenna, Petrus von Ravenna, the same name in every language that prints him.
suggested_refs: The city of Ravenna in the 1440s, under Venetian rule since 1441
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Padua, the school of Alessandro Tartagni
stops.date_confidence: attested for the teacher and the faculty (en.wikipedia; Treccani); the year of arrival is inferred from the November 1468 demonstration and is an ordering estimate [R]. The pin is the atlas's canonical Padua university pin. Palazzo Bo did not become the university's seat until 1493 (en.wikipedia, 'University of Padua'), so it was not his lecture hall.
stops.campa: He comes up the Po plain to Padua to read law under Alessandro Tartagni da Imola, consiliator, professor of civil law at Padua and at Bologna. The university has no single seat yet; the building that will house it is twenty-five years off, so the lectures happen in rented rooms scattered through the quarter and the students carry everything they own between them. Peter is carrying something else. He is already stocking, in his head, the rooms he will describe two decades later: churches walked through three or four times until the walls are learned by heart.
suggested_refs: Alessandro Tartagni da Imola (1424-1477), consiliator and professor of civil law at Padua and Bologna
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Padua, the feat on Saint Catherine's Day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie ('Petrus Ravennas', de.wikisource) independently carries 25 November 1468, the feast of St Catherine, at Padua, so the scene does not rest on Peter's own account alone; the research pool had tagged it [R] and that is corrected to [A] here. No university protocol of the event has been located [gap].
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint Catherine, before both universities assembled, a student of about twenty recites passages of Roman law from memory with their glosses and the opinions of the doctors attached, verbatim, one after another. Tartagni is said to have crossed himself before he embraced him. The scene comes down twice: from Peter's own account in the Phoenix twenty-three years later, and from the standard German biography, which gives the same feast and the same date and does not appear to be copying him.
stops.quote: Nor did I have a teacher in this artful memory, but with God assisting me, I found these most beautiful rules with the greatest labors.
stops.quote_source: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), p. 5
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie 25, 'Petrus Ravennas', on the St Catherine's Day recitation
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Padua, the licence in Roman law
stops.date_confidence: attested. Deutsche Biographie (gnd100958141) states directly that he obtained the licence in Roman law at Padua in 1471; the research pool had this as [R] on the ground that NDB was not fetched, and it has since been fetched [A]. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Three years after the feat he takes the licence in Roman law, the step short of the doctorate. It is the least dramatic entry in his life and one of the most securely dated: the German biographical dictionary states it flatly, 1471, licence in Roman law, Padua. Between the recitation before both universities and that single line there is nothing else on record. No month, no day, no subject, no teacher named, no fellow candidate. Every later account walks past the three years without a word about them.
suggested_refs: Deutsche Biographie, gnd100958141, career table for Petrus Ravennas
sources: Deutsche Biographie / Neue Deutsche Biographie, gnd100958141

stops.name: Padua, doctor of both laws
stops.date_confidence: attested (Treccani; corroborated by en.wikipedia and Deutsche Biographie). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He takes the doctorate in civil and canon law together, doctor iuris utriusque, the credential that will pay for the rest of his life. From this year every testimonial, privilege and title page calls him Doctor of Both Laws before it says anything about memory. The memory is what draws the crowds and the safe-conducts; the doctorate is what gets him the chairs. Every post he holds for the next thirty-six years, in Italy and in Germany, is a post in law.
suggested_refs: The Paduan doctorate in utroque iure and its examination procedure
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Venice, the oration for Doge Nicolo Tron
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the printer (Treccani). The research pool carried a qualifier 'after 25 February 1472' that no consulted source supports; Nicolo Tron's dogeship (elected 1471, died 28 July 1473) brackets the year but yields no day. Reduced to the year here.
stops.campa: In the year of his doctorate a short civic oration of his is printed at Venice by Nicolas Jenson, addressed to Doge Nicolo Tron: Oratio pro patria, a speech on behalf of Ravenna. He is twenty-four and in print nineteen years before the book that will make him famous. He will spend the rest of his working life handing manuscripts to printers, in Venice, Padua, Lubeck, Leipzig, Cologne and Mainz. This first one goes to Jenson, whose roman type is the finest cut in Europe.
suggested_refs: Oratio pro patria ad illustrissimum principem Nicolaum Tronum (Venice: Nicolas Jenson, 1472)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Bologna, lecturing on the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested that he lectured at Bologna, Pavia and Ferrara (Treccani, 'Pavia, Bologna e Pistoia'; ADB, lectures at Bologna, Pavia and Ferrara). The research pool cited en.wikipedia for Bologna and Pavia; that article mentions neither, and the citation is corrected here. No source gives years, so 1475 is an ordering estimate [R].
stops.campa: Before he is thirty he is lecturing at Bologna, the oldest law faculty in Christendom, on a circuit that also takes in Pavia and Ferrara. He is paid by the town and not by a career; the medieval jurist moves where the stipend is, and the stipend follows reputation. Peter's reputation is double from the start, the doctor and the prodigy in one man. The Italian and German traditions agree that he spoke to applause in all these places. Neither says what he taught there, or for how long, or where he slept.
suggested_refs: The Bolognese law faculty in the 1470s
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Pisa, the Florentine Studio and 355 florins
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB gives Pisa 1477-1479 at a stipend of 355 gulden; NDB gives Florence, Pisa and Pistoia together for 1477-1481; Treccani places him at Pistoia for the same years. The research pool framed Pisa and Pistoia as competing traditions in tension; NDB holds both at once and the tension language is dropped here.
stops.campa: The Florentine Studio, moved out of Florence to Pisa by the republic, pays him 355 florins for two years of teaching. It is the first hard number in his life: not a title, not an anecdote, a stipend. In the same span he is at Pistoia, and the two are not rivals for the same years; the modern German biography holds Florence, Pisa and Pistoia together from 1477 to 1481. What he lectured on in any of the three, and how he divided the weeks between them, is not recorded anywhere consulted.
suggested_refs: The Studio Fiorentino in exile at Pisa, 1473-1503
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Pistoia, the citizenship and the thirty years
stops.date_confidence: the grant is attested: Treccani places him at Pistoia 1477-1481 and says he gained citizenship there, and the letter itself is printed with the Phoenix. The research pool alleged a discrepancy with Treccani over 'Pisan citizenship'; Treccani says no such thing and the alleged conflict is deleted. The precise date 12 September 1480 and the thirty-year term come from the printed letter alone [R for the date].
stops.campa: The priors and the gonfalonier of justice of Pistoia grant him and his descendants the citizenship of the town, the right to hold any civic office, and thirty years' exemption from taxes yet to be imposed. The letter, printed later at the front of the Phoenix, gives its reason without embarrassment: his singular knowledge, his admirable memory, the integrity of his morals. It is the memory that buys the tax exemption. The original grant has not been traced; the date and the term come from the printed copy alone. A girl of this town, Juniper, will turn up in that same book thirty years on, lodged among the letters of his alphabet.
stops.quote: Since, therefore, our Pistoian people have for a long time accurately perceived your singular knowledge, admirable memory, and the remarkable integrity of your civil morals... it was decreed to you and your descendants the benefit of our citizenship, with the full faculty of obtaining any offices of the city, and with the exemption and immunity for the next thirty years from any payments which might hereafter be imposed.
stops.quote_source: The Priors and Gonfaloniere of Justice of Pistoia, civic letter of 12 September 1480, printed with Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), pp. 2-3
suggested_refs: The Pistoian grant of citizenship, printed among the testimonials prefixed to the Phoenix
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

segments.name: The Padua Chair and the Testimonials

stops.name: Padua, the chair in canon law at eighty ducats
stops.date_confidence: the sources disagree and are not reconciled here. Treccani: Padua from 1482-1483, initial salary 80 ducats. NDB: returned to Padua as ordinary professor from late 1483. de.wikipedia: professor of canon law at Padua from late 1479. The 80-ducat figure is firm in Treccani; the starting year is not settled. Dated 1482 to order the segment.
stops.campa: He comes back to the faculty where he was a student and takes a chair in canon law at eighty ducats. This is the longest settled stretch of his life, some fifteen years in one city, and what survives of it is mostly a record of raises. When it begins nobody agrees. The Italian dictionary says 1482 or 1483; the modern German dictionary says late 1483; German Wikipedia says he had the canon law chair from late 1479. The salary figure is the same in all of them. Which year he walked back into Padua is still open.
suggested_refs: The Paduan rolls of stipends for the law faculty, 1480s
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Padua, the salary raised to a hundred and fifty
stops.date_confidence: attested (Treccani, which gives the rise from 80 to 150 ducats in 1484). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Within two years the eighty ducats become a hundred and fifty. Padua is bidding for him against nobody in particular and everybody in general: a professor with a demonstrable prodigy attached to him draws students, and students are the university's revenue. He is travelling to perform by now as well as teaching, and the raises and the safe-conducts belong to one trade. The rolls give the figure and nothing else. No vote survives, no argument, no rector on the other side of it.
suggested_refs: Venetian salary decrees for the Studio of Padua under the Riformatori
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Padua, Matthaeus Cerdonis prints the Carmina
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Treccani carries the Carmina as printed at Padua by Matthaeus Cerdonis around 1485; the research pool tagged the item [R] and no copy or catalogue record was examined for this file. The shop's location within Padua is not established.
stops.campa: Matthaeus Cerdonis, a Bohemian printer working in Padua for the student trade, prints a collection of Peter's Latin verse. Nobody reads it now. It is the second thing he puts into print, and it sets the pattern of the rest: wherever he holds a chair he finds the local press and gives it something. The address of the shop within the city is not known. No copy of the Carmina has come under the eye of this research, which takes the book on Treccani's word and no other.
suggested_refs: Matthaeus Cerdonis of Windischgratz, printing at Padua c. 1482-1487
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Casale Monferrato, the marquis asks safe passage
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the original document, which was not located; the text is known from the testimonials printed with the Phoenix, read in translation for this file. Not carried by Treccani, ADB, NDB or any Wikipedia consulted. The date 23 September 1487 is the printed letter's own.
stops.campa: Bonifacio, Marquis of Montferrat, issues a testimonial for the doctor of both laws and Caesarean soldier Peter de Tomasius of Ravenna, who publicly teaches canon law at Padua, and asks free and safe passage for him and his party. The marquis states that he has seen the memory work himself and wonderfully experienced it. Peter keeps the document, and four years later, when the Phoenix goes to press, he prints it at the front of the book with three others. The original has not been located in any archive. The text used here is the one Peter printed.
stops.quote: And so, paying attention to the distinguished virtues, skill in the sciences, and great memory, as we ourselves have seen and wonderfully experienced, of the respectable and excellent Doctor of both Laws and Caesarean soldier, Lord Peter de Tomasius of Ravenna, who publicly teaches Canon Law at Padua...
stops.quote_source: Bonifacius, Marquis of Montferrat, testimonial of 23 September 1487, printed with Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), pp. 1-2
suggested_refs: The testimonials prefixed to the Phoenix, printed Venice 1491
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Pavia, the letter of Lancellotto Decio
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Known only from the letter printed with the Phoenix, read in translation for this file; no independent record located. Dated by the letter's own '5 Ides of November 1488', here normalized to 9 November. Note a discrepancy the research pool flagged and did not resolve: the dossier summarized this as a letter praising Peter's prodigious memory, while the translated text is a courtesy note that praises nothing.
stops.campa: A jurist of Pavia writes to him at Padua by way of a brother-in-law travelling that road, and there is almost nothing in the letter: a man should not arrive empty-handed, so here is a letter, and if you are well I rejoice, I am well. Peter prints it with the Phoenix among the testimonials to his memory. The dossier tradition calls it a letter praising his prodigious memory. The text as read praises nothing, reports nothing, and asks for nothing. He printed it anyway.
stops.quote: It was not right that my brother-in-law, coming to Padua, should come to you empty without my letters, by which, although I have nothing else to write, I at least have this which is most often placed at the beginning of epistles: if you are well, I rejoice; I am well.
stops.quote_source: Lancellottus Decius to Peter of Ravenna, 5 Ides of November 1488, printed with Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), p. 3
suggested_refs: Lancellottus Decius (Lancellotto Decio) of Pavia, jurist
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Ferrara, the duchess bears witness
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the original document, which was not located; the text is known from the testimonials printed with the Phoenix. Treccani supports a general Este connection but does not carry this letter. No existing atlas journey file documents an Este court stop against which to cross-check the 1491 episode [gap].
stops.campa: At the Castello Estense he performs before Ercole I d'Este and Eleonora of Aragon, reciting sermons from memory, and the duchess issues him a ducal testimonial: he is received among her retainers, and free passage is asked for him, his servants, his horses, his books and his silver. She writes it as a witness statement rather than a compliment, saying the whole city can bear witness too. Three months later the book is on a Venetian press with her letter bound into the front of it.
stops.quote: Which indeed he himself has lately most amply proven, so that not only we, but also this whole city of ours, can bear witness.
stops.quote_source: Eleonora of Aragon, Duchess of Ferrara, ducal testimonial of 10 October 1491, printed with Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), p. 1
suggested_refs: The Castello Estense at Ferrara under Ercole I d'Este and Eleonora of Aragon
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Venice, the demonstration circuit and Cassandra Fedele
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The meeting is attributed in the dossier to Treccani but did not surface in the Treccani text as fetched, and the en.wikipedia article on Cassandra Fedele does not mention Peter of Ravenna. The research pool tagged the identical claim [A] in one place and [R] in another; it is reduced to [R] here. The year 1490 orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Venice is where the demonstrations pay. He performs there through the late 1480s and into the 1490s, and in the course of one of these meets Cassandra Fedele, the young Venetian humanist who had disputed in Latin at Padua and to whom half of Italy wrote letters. Nothing survives of what passed between them: no correspondence, no exchange, no second occasion. The meeting itself is thin. It is attributed to Treccani and does not appear in the Treccani text as fetched, and Fedele's own article does not mention him at all.
suggested_refs: Cassandra Fedele (1465-1558), Venetian humanist and public orator
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai' (dossier attribution, not located in the fetched text)

stops.name: Venice, the privilege of the third of January
stops.date_confidence: attested for the privilege and its date (Cambridge, The Memory Arts in Renaissance England; en.wikipedia). The 'first copyright' claim is [R] and is a modern popularization: Venice had already granted an author's privilege to Marcantonio Sabellico in 1486.
stops.campa: The Venetian Senate grants Peter's chosen printer the exclusive right to print and sell the Phoenix within the dominions of the republic, and forbids anyone else to do it. Modern accounts, Italian Wikipedia among them, call this the first known example of copyright. It is not. Venice had granted an author's privilege to Marcantonio Sabellico five years earlier, in 1486, and the Sabellico grant is not in dispute. Why the Phoenix and not that one became the story people repeat, nobody consulted has explained.
suggested_refs: The Venetian privilege system for printed books, from the Sabellico grant of 1486
sources: Cambridge, The Memory Arts in Renaissance England, 'Peter of Ravenna, The Phoenix (1548)'

stops.name: Venice, the Phoenix off the press of Bernardinus de Choris
stops.date_confidence: attested: privilege 3 January, colophon 10 January, both Venetian style, sometimes normalized by incunable cataloguing to 1491/92 (Treccani; it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia). The descent of Peter's loci-and-images method from the Simonides story as Cicero transmits it in De Oratore is the standing account of the ars memorativa and is not in dispute, but the pages of the Phoenix read for this file do not themselves name Cicero or Simonides [R for the direct citation].
stops.campa: Bernardinus de Choris of Cremona finishes the book seven days after the privilege. Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria: a short manual of the art of memory, in print, available to anyone with the price of it. What had passed mouth to ear among rhetors since Simonides of Ceos named the crushed guests at Crannon by where each had reclined, and which Cicero set down in De Oratore as a story about places holding whatever is put in them, is now a commodity with a colophon. The colophon is dated the tenth of January, Venetian style.
suggested_refs: Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria (Venice: Bernardinus de Choris, 1491), ISTC record
Cicero, De Oratore II.86.351-354, on Simonides at Crannon
Quintilian, Institutio oratoria XI.2.11-17
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Venice, the church walked three or four times
stops.date_confidence: the method is quoted from the book itself (English translation, artofmemory.com edition, pp. 5-6) [A for the text]. The date is an ordering device inside the Phoenix segment and marks no event; the translator is not named on the pages fetched [gap].
stops.campa: The method takes three sentences to state and a life to stock. Take a church you know well. Walk through it three or four times looking hard at its parts, go home, and turn it over in your mind until you can walk it without being there. Then set things in it, one to a place, in order, and go and fetch them when you want them. That is the whole of the art, as he states it, and the book is not much longer than that. He claims a hundred thousand such places, with ten thousand more added since, and says that leaving home to see the cities of Italy costs him nothing, because he takes the whole of it with him.
stops.quote: I prepared for myself one hundred thousand places, and now I have added to them ten thousand, in which I have placed the things to be said by me, so that they may be at hand when I wish to test the powers of my memory. And when I leave my homeland, so that as a pilgrim I may see the cities of Italy, I can say, "I carry all my things with me."
stops.quote_source: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), pp. 5-6
suggested_refs: Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24, the earliest surviving rules for loci and imagines
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Venice, the golden conclusion and the girls
stops.date_confidence: quoted from the book itself (English translation, artofmemory.com edition, p. 6) [A for the text]. The date is an ordering device inside the Phoenix segment and marks no event. Juniper of Pistoia is not identified in any source consulted [gap].
stops.campa: For the letters of the alphabet he keeps people. Antonius for A, Benedictus for B, a person whose name begins with the letter he wants to lodge. He calls this the golden conclusion. Then he says the thing he has kept quiet about out of modesty, which is that he uses beautiful girls, because memory is wonderfully moved by them, and that the one he has placed most often in his rooms is Juniper of Pistoia, dearest to him when he was young. A canon lawyer publishes this, in a manual for students. Who Juniper was nobody has established; she appears in no source but his book.
stops.quote: I commonly place most beautiful girls for the letters. For they greatly excite my memory. And most frequently in my places I have placed Juniper of Pistoia, most dear to me when I was a youth.
stops.quote_source: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), p. 6
suggested_refs: The 'golden conclusion' of the Phoenix, the alphabet of named persons
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Venice, the physician and the flea
stops.date_confidence: quoted from the book itself (English translation, artofmemory.com edition, p. 7) [A for the text]. The date is an ordering device inside the Phoenix segment and marks no event. Master Gherard of Verona is not otherwise identified in any source consulted [gap].
stops.campa: The rule for images is that they must strike, so he builds them out of things he has actually watched happen. For a flea he places Master Gherard of Verona, the most excellent physician of the age, because he once saw the man catch one. The whole system runs on this: not invented monsters but real people caught in a single absurd instant and nailed to a spot on a wall. Gherard is not identified in anything consulted, and no other mention of him has been found. He survives as a doctor, somewhere in a wall of the memory palace, pinching a flea.
stops.quote: I very often for a flea have placed the most excellent physician of all our age, Master Gherard of Verona, whom I once saw catching a flea.
stops.quote_source: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com edition), p. 7
suggested_refs: The doctrine of imagines agentes, striking images, in the Rhetorica ad Herennium and its Renaissance heirs
sources: Peter of Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria, English translation (artofmemory.com PDF edition)

stops.name: Padua, two hundred ducats for many children
stops.date_confidence: attested (Treccani, which gives an additional 50 ducats a year on account of his many children, bringing the total to 200 by this date). The second wife's name, Lucrezia Azzoni of Este, is from Treccani [A]; the research pool's note that Este is also the Este family seat is a dossier-internal observation, not corroborated by any atlas file [R].
stops.campa: The Paduan authorities add another fifty ducats a year, bringing him to two hundred, and the reason entered in the record is his many children. The Phoenix is a year old and selling; his salary now rests partly on the size of his household. He has married twice, the second time to Lucrezia Azzoni, from Este. The children are numerous enough to appear as a line in a university budget. How many there were the record does not say. It says many, and it pays.
suggested_refs: Paduan stipend records naming the increase pro multis liberis
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

segments.name: Over the Alps: the Baltic Years

stops.name: Padua, the summons from Pomerania
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and for Bogislaw X's role (Treccani; en.wikipedia; NDB). The month 'November' carried by the research pool is supported by no consulted source and is dropped. The story that Bogislaw first heard Peter praised while stopping at Venice on his return from the Holy Land is dossier-only and no consulted source carries it [R].
stops.campa: Bogislaw X, Duke of Pomerania, wants a jurist of European name for his university at Greifswald, and picks the professor at Padua whose memory has been talked about for thirty years. Peter accepts. At forty-nine he leaves the Italian world he has never once lived outside, and takes his wife, his children and his books with him. The tradition that the duke first heard him praised at Venice on the way home from Jerusalem is dossier material and no biography consulted repeats it.
suggested_refs: Bogislaw X of Pomerania (1454-1523) and the University of Greifswald
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Innsbruck, the night audience with Maximilian
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB carries the episode directly, including that the king sent for him at night while holding court at Innsbruck and dismissed him with honours and the title eques auratus; the research pool tagged it [R] and that is corrected here. Two corrections to the pool: the title belongs to Maximilian I at Innsbruck in 1497, not to Frederick III in 1487, and Frederick III appears nowhere in this connection. Month and day unrecorded.
stops.campa: The road north goes through Innsbruck, where Maximilian I is holding court, and the king, hearing who has come through his town, sends for him at night. Peter performs: poetry and legal allegations, out of his head, in a hall that had not expected him that evening and does not send him away until it is finished. He is dismissed with honours and with the title eques auratus, golden knight, which he will put on his title pages for the rest of his life. He goes on toward the Baltic in the morning with the family and the books.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie 25, 'Petrus Ravennas', on the Innsbruck audience and the eques auratus

stops.name: Greifswald, matriculation and the rectorate in five weeks
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB gives arrival in April 1498 with his family, matriculation 24 April, and the rectorate on 3 May 1498; Treccani gives the April arrival. The research pool cited en.wikipedia for the arrival, which does not describe it; the citation is corrected. The 1456 founding ceremony in the cathedral of St Nicholas is from en.wikipedia, 'University of Greifswald'.
stops.campa: He arrives in April with his wife and children, matriculates on the twenty-fourth, and by the third of May he is rector of the university. Five weeks from Italian professor to head of a Pomeranian studium. Greifswald is a brick town on a river three miles short of the Baltic, made a university forty-two years earlier in the cathedral of St Nicholas, and it is nothing whatever like Padua. He teaches both laws. He will hold the rectorate here twice.
suggested_refs: Dom St. Nikolai, Greifswald, where the university was founded in 1456
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Lubeck, Lucas Brandis prints the Repetitio
stops.date_confidence: attested. de.wikipedia's works list gives 'Repeticio c. inter alia de emunitate ecclesiae' (Lubeck: Lucas Brandis, 1499); the research pool had this as unverified dossier tradition with no printer, and both the attestation and the printer are corrected in. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Lucas Brandis prints at Lubeck Peter's Repetitio on the clause inter alia, on the immunity of the church: a canon lawyer's treatise on how far ecclesiastical privilege reaches and where exactly it stops. He is in the Hanseatic north now and the presses he uses are Hanseatic ones, a hundred and thirty miles from the university that pays him. It is an ordinary professional book, the kind of work that took up most of his days and none of his reputation. Brandis had been printing at Lubeck since 1475.
suggested_refs: Repeticio c. inter alia de emunitate ecclesiae (Lubeck: Lucas Brandis, 1499)

stops.name: Greifswald, rector a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB gives both rectorates (3 May 1498 and spring 1501) and NDB likewise (1498 and 1501); Treccani gives only 1501 and does not contradict 1498. The research pool framed this as two rival datings of one rectorate; there were two rectorates and the framing is corrected. The son Giambattista's matriculation in 1502 is dossier-only [R].
stops.campa: In the spring he is rector again. Three years in the town have made him its most conspicuous scholar, and the office comes back to him. His son Giambattista matriculates here the following year, which is dossier tradition and not confirmed by any biography consulted. The family is putting down roots in a place none of them chose, on a coast where the winters are longer than anything in the Romagna. What the second rectorate consisted of, or what he did with it, no record consulted says.
suggested_refs: The Greifswald rectorate lists for 1498 and 1501
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Greifswald, the death of Marieta
stops.date_confidence: attested for the name and the day: ADB gives the daughter as Marieta, died 25 October 1502 at Greifswald. The research pool called her Margherita and placed an epidemic around her that killed several of his other children; ADB describes no epidemic and no other children's deaths, and that part is [R] and is not carried as fact here.
stops.campa: His daughter Marieta dies on the twenty-fifth of October. The German biography gives the name and the day and then stops: no cause, no burial place, no epitaph. The dossier called her Margherita and put an epidemic around her that carried off several of his other children as well; no source consulted supports either the epidemic or the other deaths. One name and one day is the whole of what is known about her, which is more than is known about any of her brothers and sisters except the two sons who matriculate.

stops.name: Leipzig, the Aurea opuscula
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani gives Aurea opuscula, Leipzig 1502; Wolfgang Stockel is independently attested as running a Leipzig press from 1495 into the 1520s. The research pool tagged this [R] as dossier-only and that is corrected. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Wolfgang Stockel prints at Leipzig the Aurea opuscula, the golden little works, gathering the Phoenix together with shorter Latin pieces into a single volume. The memory manual is now the anchor of a collected edition and plainly the thing his name sells; the poems and the legal pieces ride in on it. Eleven years after Venice the book has crossed the Alps and found a German market without its author having to stand up in front of anyone. Peter is at Greifswald that year, burying a daughter.
suggested_refs: Aurea opuscula (Leipzig: Wolfgang Stockel, 1502)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Wittenberg, the lecture on the two powers
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB records a public lecture at Wittenberg on 3 May 1503 on the power of the pope and of the Roman emperor, and the sermones extraordinarii; NDB and Treccani carry the Wittenberg appointment from 1503. The research pool cited en.wikipedia, which does not mention Wittenberg at all, and that citation is corrected. The pin is the atlas's canonical Leucorea pin. The son Vincentius as rector in spring 1504 is from ADB.
stops.campa: Frederick the Wise founded a university at Wittenberg the year before and is buying faculty. Peter takes a law chair, and on the third of May he delivers a public lecture on the power of the supreme pontiff and of the Roman emperor: the oldest question in canon law, put by a new professor at a university with no traditions of its own yet. He also gives extraordinary lectures on religious and moral subjects, which is not what a law chair is for. His son Vincentius is rector of the place within the year.
suggested_refs: The Leucorea, founded 1502 by Frederick the Wise, Elector of Saxony
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Wittenberg, the plague and the road west
stops.date_confidence: attested that he left in the summer of 1506 (de.wikipedia) and that plague is the reason given (Treccani). The research pool gave 'July 1506' and said the university formally dispersed; no consulted source specifies the month or says that, and both are dropped. Dated 1 June 1506 to mark the summer.
stops.campa: Plague reaches Wittenberg in the summer of 1506 and he leaves. It is the third university he has quit in nine years, and the pattern of the German decade is fixed by now: arrive with a reputation, teach, publish with whatever press the town has, move on when something breaks. He is fifty-eight years old and still telling people he means to get back to Italy. Every move he makes carries him further west and north instead. No source consulted says the university dispersed. What they say is that he went.
suggested_refs: The 1506 plague at Wittenberg
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Cologne, matriculation on the third of December
stops.date_confidence: attested (Deutsche Biographie, gnd100958141, which gives the matriculation date and the warm initial reception; en.wikipedia gives the 1506 appointment). The pin is the atlas's canonical Cologne pin, inherited from the Reuchlin, Agrippa and Cusanus files.
stops.campa: He matriculates at Cologne on the third of December and begins teaching civil and canon law. The reception is warm: professors, humanists, prominent citizens of a large rich city holding the biggest university in the Empire and a Dominican house at the middle of it. He is the most famous jurist to arrive in years and the town treats him accordingly. What terms he came on, nothing consulted says. The register has the date, the name and the faculty, and stops there.

stops.name: Cologne, the Third Order of Saint Francis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact. ADB confirms it from the book's own colophon matter, that he and his wife had entered the order of Tertiaries under the rule of St Francis; Treccani and en.wikipedia carry it and Treccani supplies the wife's name, Lucrezia Azzoni. The research pool tagged it [R] as dossier-only and that is corrected. The precise year 1507 remains soft; month and day unrecorded.
stops.campa: He and Lucrezia take the habit of the Third Order of Saint Francis, the rule for lay people who stay in the world. The statement of it comes from the colophon matter of one of his own books, which is to say that he announced it in print, the way he announced everything. The year is soft, the month and day are unrecorded, and no house of the order at Cologne is named as the place of profession. He is fifty-nine, a doctor of both laws and a golden knight of the Empire, and sixteen years earlier he had published that he stocked his memory with beautiful girls.

stops.name: Cologne, the bodies left on the gallows
stops.date_confidence: attested for the dispute and the antagonist (en.wikipedia; de.wikipedia, 'contrary to natural and divine law'; ADB, which also has the parallel quarrel over whether tithes are iuris divini). Ortwin Gratius's defence in the Criticomastix is from ADB [A]; the pool's added claim that Gratius later switched sides appears in no consulted source and is not carried [R, dropped]. Gerardus de Zutphania as a co-antagonist is likewise unattested outside the dossier [R]. Dated mid-1507 to order the segment.
stops.campa: He argues in public that to leave the corpse of an executed criminal unburied, when the man had repented and been absolved, is against natural and divine law and a mortal sin. The Dominican Jacob van Hoogstraten, prior of the Cologne house, answers him. A faculty commission warns that his propositions may be punishable. Ortwin Gratius defends him in the Criticomastix. The quarrel runs a year, and at the bottom of it is a dead man's body, hanging where the city left it.
suggested_refs: Jacob van Hoogstraten's Justificatorium / Protectorium principum Alamaniae
Ortwin Gratius, Criticomastix

stops.name: Cologne, the heirs of Quentell print the Alphabetum aureum
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book (Treccani; de.wikipedia, 'Alphabetum aureum utriusque juris, Cologne 1508'). Printer corrected: the research pool gave Heinrich Quentell, who died 10 August 1501 and cannot have printed a 1508 book; the imprint belongs to his heirs, who printed as Quentell Erben until Peter Quentell took sole control around 1520. A feudal-law compendium is placed at Cologne 1508 in one pool item and at Mainz 1508 in another; see the Mainz stop, where it is downgraded [R].
stops.campa: The Alphabetum aureum utriusque iuris comes off a Cologne press: an alphabetical reference to both laws, look up the word and find the law under it. It is the most practical thing he ever made and it runs on the same instinct as the memory book, which also sorts the world by first letters and fetches by them. The shop is the Quentell house, though Heinrich Quentell himself has been dead seven years by now and the imprint belongs to his heirs, who go on printing under that name until Peter Quentell takes it over around 1520.
suggested_refs: Alphabetum aureum utriusque iuris (Cologne: heirs of Heinrich Quentell, 1508)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Cologne, Palm Sunday and the ship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the farewell sermon on Palm Sunday, 16 April 1508, and the departure by ship on 27 April (en.wikipedia). The remark about Italian students is reported speech and NOT a quotation: Theodor Muther, 'Ausgang des Petrus Ravennas' (1866), pp. 114-115, translates the close of Peter's own 1508 pamphlet Valete cum perpetuo silentio and prints only German, so no Latin wording is verifiable and none is given here. Per ADB this remark was a late flashpoint, not the origin of the Hoogstraten quarrel.
stops.campa: On Palm Sunday he preaches a farewell sermon, and eleven days later, on the twenty-seventh of April, he goes down the Rhine by ship. He is sixty and leaving under attack, having arrived two years earlier as the celebrated Italian. He is also still arguing. By his own parting pamphlet he had said, in speech and in writing and in jest, that Italian students cannot live without prostitutes, and men who hung on his mouth to catch him at something had begun crying crucify him, crucify him.
suggested_refs: Peter of Ravenna, Valete cum perpetuo silentio ad ... Jacobum de Alta platea (1508)

stops.name: Mainz, the old university beside the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment as ordinarius in canon law in the summer of 1508 (ADB; NDB). PIN CORRECTED: the research pool placed this at 49.9929/8.2473, which is the modern Johannes Gutenberg University campus, built on a 1938 barracks site and opened as a university in 1946; the university Peter joined was the old University of Mainz, founded 1477, in the Altstadt beside the cathedral, about 2.2 km northeast. The Johann Schoffer imprint of Contra Gherardum de Zutphania et fratrem Jacobum is dossier-only and unverified [R]. The 'Compendium breve' on feudal custom that the pool placed here is downgraded: en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia both give Compendium juris civilis et canonici as a Cologne imprint of Hermann Bungart, 1507 [R for the Mainz attribution].
stops.campa: He takes an ordinary chair in canon law at Mainz in the summer, at the university founded in 1477 beside the cathedral in the old town, and goes on answering Hoogstraten in print from there. Johann Schoffer, whose father printed with Gutenberg's own types, is said to have printed the reply, though only the dossier says so and no copy has been traced. The city is a Rhine archbishopric and the seat of the Empire's senior elector, and the Cologne quarrel has followed him upriver. He is sixty years old.
suggested_refs: The old University of Mainz, founded 1477, dissolved 1798
Contra Gherardum de Zutphania et fratrem Jacobum theologie professores (Mainz: Johann Schoffer, 1508), unverified

stops.name: Mainz, the Carmelites and the charge of fornication
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The episode is unattested in ADB, NDB, Treccani or any Wikipedia consulted, and rests on the dossier alone. PIN CORRECTED: the pool gave 49.9968/8.2717; the Karmeliterkirche stands at Karmeliterplatz 5, 50.0027/8.2733, about 660 m north. The date is an ordering estimate; only the year is claimed even in the dossier.

He condemns it flatly, and then improvises, they say, out of the Epistle to the Hebrews, at whatever length the occasion required: the memory turned to his own defence, standing up, in a strange city, with no book in front of him. None of this is attested. It rests on the dossier alone, and no biography consulted mentions the occasion, the audience or the cardinal.

stops.name: Worms, advocate at the Imperial Chamber Court
stops.date_confidence: attested with independent structural corroboration. NDB states he became an advocate at the Reichskammergericht at Worms in autumn 1509; de.wikipedia's Reichskammergericht article confirms the court sat at Regensburg 1503-1509 and returned to Worms in 1509, where it stayed to 1513. The research pool tagged this [R]; it is upgraded. Dated 1 September to mark the autumn. The pin is the atlas's canonical Worms pin; the courtroom building is not identified [gap].
stops.campa: In the autumn he becomes an advocate at the Reichskammergericht, the Imperial Chamber Court, which had sat at Regensburg since 1503 and came back to Worms in this same year. He is sixty-one and no longer teaching. The last recorded work of his life is ordinary practice: appearing before the highest court in the Empire on other men's cases. Not one of those cases is named. The courtroom has not been identified either, and the pin here is the town.

stops.name: Worms, the death between two years
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a range. Treccani: died between 1509 and 1510, at Worms; Deutsche Biographie concurs. The older tradition placing his death at Mainz in 1508 is treated by Treccani as superseded. No day, no month, no cause is recorded anywhere consulted. Dated 1510-01-01 by convention, not by evidence.
stops.campa: He dies between 1509 and 1510, probably here, past sixty years old. There is no date, no cause, no deathbed and no witness on record anywhere. The older shorthand had him dying at Mainz in 1508, and the Italian biography now treats that as superseded without replacing it with anything narrower than a two-year window. He had left Ravenna at about twenty to study law and never got back to it; the last twelve years ran through Greifswald, Wittenberg, Cologne, Mainz and Worms, and in every one of them he told people he was going home.
suggested_refs: Treccani's dating, 'Mori tra il 1509 e il 1510', at Worms
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Pietro Francesco Tomai'

stops.name: Worms, the grave that is not there
stops.date_confidence: the absence is a confirmed negative finding, not an inference: en.wikipedia, it.wikipedia and de.wikipedia all stop at the death year with no burial detail, and a targeted search for grave, tomb and monument returned nothing in Worms or Ravenna. The dossier never mentions a tomb either. Dated only to close the segment; it marks no event.
stops.campa: No tomb, no marker, no burial church, no monument. Three encyclopedias in three languages, and a search made specifically for grave, tomb and monument, turn up nothing at all, in Worms or in Ravenna: no slab, no plaque, no bust, no street carrying the name. The man who built himself a hundred thousand rooms and could walk to anything he had ever put in any of them left no address of his own for anybody to walk to. Every source consulted ends at the year and says nothing further.
suggested_refs: The absence of any recorded burial place for Petrus Ravennas

stops.name: Cologne, the letter of Johann Reuchlin
stops.date_confidence: attested. ADB directly confirms Reuchlin's letter of 1 November 1518 to Cardinal Achille de Grassis attributing Peter's death to Hoogstraten's persecution; the research pool hedged this as a legend only loosely supported, and the hedge is corrected. The Latin phrase 'prae maerore' was not located in any primary text and is not quoted here [R for the wording]. The letter concerns the Cologne expulsion, so the stop sits at Peter's Cologne pin; Reuchlin's own writing of it belongs on Reuchlin's file, not this one.
stops.campa: Ten years after the ship left the Rhine quay, Johann Reuchlin writes to Cardinal Achille de Grassis that the divine Petrus Ravennas perished from grief after Hoogstraten drove him out of Cologne. Reuchlin is by then five years into his own prosecution by the same Dominican, so he is not a disinterested witness; and Peter did not die at Cologne, having taught two more years at Mainz and pleaded at Worms after he left. The letter is real and dated and has been quoted ever since. Nobody has produced a contemporary account of the death to check it against.
suggested_refs: Johann Reuchlin to Cardinal Achille de Grassis, 1 November 1518

stops.date_confidence: [R] for the 1533 Venice reprint: named in the dossier as printed by Giovanni Antonio Nicolini da Sabbio for Melchiorre Sessa and associated with Wellcome holdings, but Wellcome and Internet Archive fetches both failed to surface the record. Bruno's boyhood reading of Peter's memory works is [A] from the Cambridge Memory Arts chapter; the pool's added claim linking Peter to Bruno's mnemonic 'seals' is not in that source and is dropped.
stops.campa: Forty-two years after the first colophon the book is still a Venetian commodity, reprinted for the bookseller Melchiorre Sessa, though this printing could not be verified: a Wellcome search and an archive.org fetch both failed to surface the record. The book generally keeps going, at Erfurt, Cologne, Paris, London and Vicenza, in Latin and in translation, for more than a century. Giordano Bruno read Peter's memory works as a boy, and took places and images off into territory their systematizer never proposed.

stops.name: London, Robert Copland puts it into English
stops.date_confidence: attested for the translation (en.wikipedia; Cambridge, The Memory Arts in Renaissance England). Bibliographers date it variously 1545 or about 1548 and do not agree; 1548 is used here to order the segment. The French translation, L'art de memoire qui est aultrement inscript le phenix, Paris 1545, is [R] on en.wikipedia's bare listing.
stops.campa: Robert Copland, printer and translator in London, puts the book into English as An Art of Memory That Otherwise Is Called the Phoenix. Bibliographers date it 1545 or about 1548 and do not agree with each other. A French version, L'art de memoire qui est aultrement inscript le phenix, had come out at Paris. The rooms Peter walked in Italian churches are being stocked now in English, by readers who have the rules and nothing else about the man who wrote them. Whether Copland worked from the Latin or from the French is not established.

stops.name: Vicenza, still in print after a century
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the Vicenza 1600 (Pietro Bertelli) and Cologne 1608 printings, which are named only in the dossier's editions list and were not independently confirmed within this session's search budget. The omission from the general encyclopedic survey of the art of memory is [A]: the en.wikipedia 'Art of memory' article was fetched and checked, and does not mention Peter of Ravenna anywhere.
stops.campa: A hundred and nine years after the first colophon, Pietro Bertelli prints the Phoenix at Vicenza, and a Cologne printing follows in 1608. Neither has been confirmed outside the dossier's editions list. The book outlives the quarrels, the chairs, the safe-conducts, the daughter buried at Greifswald, and the man. The general encyclopedic survey of the art of memory that most people read today, running from antiquity through the seventeenth century, was fetched and checked for this file. It does not mention him once.
